Adding a second classifier: global vs. local database reconciliation

Source: vignettes/REGATTA-two-database.Rmd
REGATTA-two-database.Rmd

This vignette covers Module 3 of REGATTA: reconciling the same ASVs classified against two reference databases, a broad global one and a locally curated one, to keep the benefits of both, then reconciling the result against the regional checklist.

It builds on vignette("REGATTA-tutorial"), which covers Module 1 (building and taxonomizing the regional checklist) and Module 2 (reconciling one classifier against it). Start there first. Module 3 inserts one extra step, reconcile_global_local(), ahead of the Module 2 checklist reconciliation, and run_regatta() runs both in a single call.

When you’d use this

Module 2 reconciles the output of one classifier against the regional checklist. Module 3 lets you combine two classifiers — one run against a global reference database and one run against a local database — into a single taxonomy table that keeps the advantages of both.

A global reference database (for this tutorial, we used a MiFish obitools database made with all vertebrate sequences from EMBL) contains species from all over the world. A local reference database (here, vsearch assignments against a regional reference database created by downloading mitochondrial sequences from NCBI for the local checklist of species produced in Module 1) contains only the species that occur in your region, so it is a subset of the global one.

The local database has two advantages:

  • It does not assign a sequence to a species that does not occur in your region.
  • When several species share the same sequence at the barcode region and one of them is the local species, it does not downgrade the assignment to a higher taxonomic level unnecessarily — it can keep the local species.

The local database also has one drawback. When the local species is missing from it, the sequence is left completely unassigned. A global database behaves differently in that case: it can match the sequence to a non-local species that has an identical barcode sequence, and Module 2 then downgrades that call to a taxonomic level that does occur in the region.

reconcile_global_local() lets you compare the assignments made for the same ASVs with a global and a local database, and merges them so you keep the advantages of both. For each ASV it keeps the call with the higher percent identity. When the global call wins but disagrees with the local one, it reports the lowest common ancestor of the two.

This vignette uses the same Galapagos MiFish dataset as the main tutorial: the identical 1,438 ASVs, classified a second time against a local database.

run_regatta()

Use run_regatta() to run the two-database workflow in one call. It runs reconcile_global_local() and then reconcile_checklist() for you, so adding a second database does not mean running a second pipeline.

Pass both results as a named list(global =, local =). Formats are auto-detected. Here the local side is a vsearch lca taxonomy file plus a --userout file carrying the percent identities.

library(REGATTA)

res <- run_regatta(
  input = list(
    global = "MiFish_obitools.tab",                 # obitools (global EMBL DB)
    local  = c("MiFish_vsearch_lca.txt",            # vsearch LCA taxonomy
               "MiFish_vsearch_userout.txt")        # vsearch %ID
  ),
  checklist = cl$for_LCA,                            # from build_regional_checklist()
  out_dir   = "regatta_out",                         # REQUIRED: dated run subfolder
  region    = "galapagos", label = "fish"            # name the run subfolder
  # sql_path defaults to the cache; pass a path to override.
)
#> returns res$taxonomy_table (final reconciled table), res$tracking (per-ASV
#> audit, both stages combined), res$summary, plus res$reconciled / res$post_checklist;
#> writes reconcile_global_local/*, reconcile_checklist/*, regatta_summary.csv,
#> run_log.txt into regatta_out/galapagos_fish_<date>/

On the full dataset, of the 1,438 ASVs, 892 were unassigned by both classifiers and 546 were assigned by at least one. Stage 1 resolved those:

ASVs
best %ID: global won 403
best %ID: local won 143
global downgraded to global∩local LCA 45

Stage 2 (the checklist) then gave 295 species, 231 genus, 19 family, and 1 order among the 546 assigned. The checklist dropped none, because every reconciled call had a regional record; the other 892 ASVs were simply unassigned by both classifiers. Compared with the main tutorial’s single-classifier obitools run (287 species), those extra species-level calls are the local database’s contribution.

reconcile_global_local()

reconcile_global_local() is the Stage 1 step that run_regatta() calls for you. Running it directly shows how each ASV’s two calls were reconciled: which won on percent identity, and what REGATTA preferred. It runs with no internet and no taxonomy database.

The demo uses real slices of the Galapagos MiFish dataset bundled with the package: 12 real ASVs classified both ways, chosen to show each decision. You would normally pass the whole tables.

library(REGATTA)

global <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "mifish_obitools_example.csv",
                               package = "REGATTA"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
local  <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "mifish_vsearch_example.csv",
                               package = "REGATTA"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

rec <- reconcile_global_local(global, local, output_dir = NULL)

$tracking shows the per-ASV decision with each field grouped global / local / regatta (the reconciled value), so you can read the two classifiers’ calls and REGATTA’s pick side by side:

rec$tracking[, c("ASV_id",
                 "species_global", "species_local", "species_regatta",
                 "pct_id_global", "pct_id_local", "pct_id_regatta",
                 "best_pctid_winner", "preferred_database")]

There are four per-ASV outcomes, with two genera shown for each:

  • Global only (the local database made no call, so the global call is kept): the six checklist-demo genera from the main tutorial, Abudefduf saxatilis / taurus, Prionurus laticlavius / biafraensis, Archosargus rhomboidalis, and Conodon nobilis. With nothing to reconcile, they pass through unchanged.
  • Both agree, so the call is kept: Lutjanus kasmira and Caranx melampygus. Both databases name the same species, and with Local_advantage = TRUE (the default) the tie goes to local. The species is kept.
  • Disagree and the global percent identity wins, so REGATTA downgrades to the LCA (global_lca_to_local): Epinephelus bontoides (global) vs. E. merra (local), and Mugil curema (global) vs. M. thoburni (local). The global call has the higher identity, but because the two conflict at species, REGATTA reports the lowest common ancestor, genus Epinephelus and genus Mugil.
  • Disagree and the local percent identity wins, so the local call is kept: Etrumeus teres (local, 99.4%) over E. micropus (global, 98.9%), and Cubiceps pauciradiatus (local) over C. squamiceps (global). Here the locally curated database has the better match, so its call is trusted outright.

Feed the reconciled result straight into the checklist step, exactly as in the single-classifier workflow:

checklist <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "galapagos_fish_checklist.rds",
                                 package = "REGATTA"))
post <- reconcile_checklist(rec$result, checklist, output_dir = NULL)

Same 12 ASVs, both methods, side by side

Whether a second database is worth it comes down to what changes versus the single-classifier run, and the changes go both ways: some calls become less specific (a conflict caught), and some become more specific (a regional species recovered).

Run the main-tutorial method (obitools straight to the checklist) on the same inputs and compare the final call:

single <- reconcile_checklist(global, checklist, output_dir = NULL)

# the most specific non-NA rank per ASV, named by ASV_id (the reconcile steps
# may reorder rows, so we key on the id rather than trusting row position)
lowest <- function(r) {
  ranks <- c("domain","phylum","class","order","family","genus","species")
  v <- apply(r$result[, ranks], 1, function(x) {nz <- which(!is.na(x)); if (length(nz)) x[max(nz)] else NA})
  stats::setNames(v, r$result$ASV_id)
}
ids <- global$ASV_id
data.frame(
  obitools_call = global$species,
  single_db     = lowest(single)[ids],
  two_db        = lowest(post)[ids],
  row.names     = NULL
)
#>               obitools_call             single_db                 two_db
#> 1       Abudefduf saxatilis   Abudefduf saxatilis    Abudefduf saxatilis
#> 2          Abudefduf taurus             Abudefduf              Abudefduf
#> 3     Prionurus laticlavius Prionurus laticlavius  Prionurus laticlavius
#> 4     Prionurus biafraensis             Prionurus              Prionurus
#> 5  Archosargus rhomboidalis              Sparidae               Sparidae
#> 6           Conodon nobilis            Haemulidae             Haemulidae
#> 7          Lutjanus kasmira      Lutjanus kasmira       Lutjanus kasmira
#> 8         Caranx melampygus     Caranx melampygus      Caranx melampygus
#> 9              Mugil curema          Mugil curema                  Mugil
#> 10    Epinephelus bontoides           Epinephelus            Epinephelus
#> 11        Etrumeus micropus     Etrumeus micropus         Etrumeus teres
#> 12      Cubiceps squamiceps              Cubiceps Cubiceps pauciradiatus

Nine of the twelve land in the same place, but three change, each in a different way:

  • Mugil curema: single-DB keeps the species (M. curema is on the checklist); two-DB drops to genus Mugil because the local database’s M. thoburni contradicts it. Two databases caught a conflict one could not.
  • Etrumeus micropus: single-DB keeps the global species; two-DB replaces it with Etrumeus teres, the local database’s higher-identity, regionally curated call.
  • Cubiceps squamiceps: single-DB downgrades to genus Cubiceps (squamiceps is not on the checklist); two-DB keeps the species Cubiceps pauciradiatus, because the local database’s call is on the checklist. Here the second database makes the result more specific, not less.

Inspecting and tuning

The reconciliation is fully auditable and adjustable. You can see why each ASV got its call, and change how ties and percent-identity scales are handled to fit your databases.

  • The full Stage 1 audit (reconcile_global_local/ on disk, or rec$tracking) groups its columns per field as <field>_global / <field>_local / <field>_regatta (the reconciled value). Each of the seven ranks and pct_id read global / local / regatta side by side, followed by the decision columns (best_pctid_winner, preferred_database, and so on) and any remaining classifier columns.
  • Local_advantage = FALSE makes ties go to the global database instead.
  • Percent-identity scales are auto-detected per input (obitools’ 0–1 BEST_IDENTITY is rescaled to 0–100 to match vsearch). Override with global_pct_id_scale / local_pct_id_scale if needed.

See ?reconcile_global_local for the full argument list, and vignette("REGATTA-tutorial") for the checklist-building steps this workflow assumes.
